title: Vaccination infodemic among citizens of Magallanes, Cavite, Philippines
screen_reason: One self-reported exposure share with a denominator: 90.4% of 157 surveyed citizens agreed with the item 'It took a while for me to get vaccinated because I read/learned from social media and/or TV/radio that vaccines were not safe and effective', i.e. they report having encountered the false claim that COVID-19 vaccines are unsafe and ineffective. Share of survey respondents who say they came across misinformation = RECALL (exposure).

estimates.platform: Self-reported exposure via social media and/or TV/radio (survey instrument)
estimates.measure_type: % of surveyed citizens who report they delayed vaccination because they read or learned from social media and/or TV/radio that COVID-19 vaccines were not safe and effective
estimates.denominator: 157 adult residents of Magallanes, Cavite who attended the municipal vaccination site on four dates and volunteered to complete the online questionnaire (20.0% of the 784 people who showed up on those dates)
estimates.definition: Agreement with the survey statement 'It took a while for me to get vaccinated because I read/learned from social media and/or TV/radio that vaccines were not safe and effective' - i.e. self-reported encounter with the (false) claim that COVID-19 vaccines are unsafe and ineffective, coupled with a self-attributed delay in getting vaccinated.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation: misleading or inaccurate information" (Greenspan & Loftus); the paper frames the object of study as the WHO 'infodemic', "the overabundance of information, which entailed deliberate attempt to distribute wrong information", with the vaccine-harm claim given as its 'one concrete example'.
estimates.source_quote: Social media and traditional media like television and radio have a wide reach and influence, thus 90.4% (Fig. 5) of the respondents delayed their time to get vaccines because they received information that COVID-19 vaccines were not safe and effective.
estimates.page_loc: Survey Results and Discussion, Fig. 5 and accompanying text, p. 60; denominator from Table 3, p. 58
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent self-report only; the falsity of the claim ('vaccines were not safe and effective') is asserted by the authors, not verified against any fact-check or external list. No item wording validation, no reliability statistics, and the underlying figure is presented only as a chart (Fig. 5) with the percentage restated in the text.
estimates.moderator_quote: The study employed survey research and gathered data using voluntary sampling from a pool of citizens with an appointment schedule in the vaccination site located in Magallanes, Cavite. Respondents answered a self-administered online questionnaire using Google forms with seven different questions translated into Filipino.
estimates.notes: TWO CAVEATS an adjudicator should see. (a) The item bundles EXPOSURE with an EFFECT: agreement means both 'I encountered the claim' and 'it delayed my vaccination', so this is a stricter measure than a plain 'did you come across misinformation' item and 90.4% cannot be read as a pure exposure rate - if anything, plain exposure would be at least this high. (b) The denominator is a self-selected convenience sample of people who were AT a vaccination site and chose to answer (157 of 784, 20.0%), i.e. vaccine accepters in one 4th-class municipality of 22,727 people; the authors themselves note the respondents are 'only 2% of the total vaccinated citizens of Magallanes'. Confidence is low: this is a short conference-proceedings paper with no reported item wording beyond the figure captions, no demographics of respondents, no analysis beyond frequencies, and no confidence intervals. platform_norm coded 'survey' because the named channel spans social media AND broadcast TV/radio, which no single platform value covers.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) NOT extracted (information sources, not misinformation exposure): 96.8% get news/information from Facebook, 68.8% from family, friends and neighbours, 67.5% from television. These are media-diet shares; they say nothing about the veracity of what was received. 2) NOT extracted (attitudes/beliefs, out of scope): 82.8% thought twice or more before getting vaccinated; 77.1% believe that once fully vaccinated they will not be infected by COVID-19 (a misperception held, i.e. belief, which the eligibility rules exclude); 86.6% would take any brand; brand preferences (Moderna 39.5%, Pfizer 24.2%, Sinovac 18.5%, Sinopharm 12.1%). 3) NOT extracted (reasons for vaccinating): 51% had no time/were not yet scheduled, 28.7% encouraged by family and friends, 24.2% work or school requirement, 15.9% travel requirement, 18.5% fear of reinfection, 6.4% fear of losing government aid. 4) NOT extracted (figure cited from elsewhere, barred by R8): '51% of Filipinos define fake news as untrue information. 46% believe it is unverified information. 37% think those are manipulated photos and videos' - from Chua, Curato and Ong (2021), not this study's data. 5) NOT extracted (not misinformation): vaccination coverage by priority group (A1 75%, A2 59%, A3 80%, A4 32%, A5 40%, total 69%) and the survey response rates by date (11.7%, 22.2%, 21.2%, 31.7%, total 20.0%). 6) Note on arithmetic: 90.4% of 157 = 141.9, so the underlying count is presumably 142; the paper gives no counts for any survey item, only percentages read off charts, so I recorded the percentage as stated rather than reconstructing a count.

rob.design: Cross-sectional, self-administered online survey (Google Forms, seven questions, translated into Filipino) with voluntary sampling of adult residents attending the Magallanes, Cavite vaccination site on four dates (23, 28, 30 September and 21 October 2021). 784 people appeared at the site on those dates and 157 completed the questionnaire, an overall take-up of 20.0% (11.7%, 22.2%, 21.2% and 31.7% by date). The frame is therefore people who had already decided to be vaccinated and had an appointment, in a municipality of 22,727 with a master list of 9,564 priority-group residents; the authors state the respondents are only 2% of the municipality's vaccinated citizens. No probability sampling, no non-response analysis, no respondent demographics reported, no pilot or item-validation described, no reliability statistics, no ethics statement, no inferential analysis - results are frequencies presented as pie/bar figures with percentages restated in the text. Veracity of the claim referenced in the exposure item is asserted by the authors rather than externally verified. Published as a library-science conference proceeding.
rob.item6_quote: Misinformation: misleading or inaccurate information (Greenspan & Loftus, 2021).
